'''''Psidium guineense''''' is a species of [[guava]].

Common names include '''Brazilian guava''', '''Castilian guava''',<ref name=purdue>[http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/brazilian_guava_ars.html Brazilian Guava (''Psidium guineense'' Sw.)] The Center for New Crops & Plant Products. Purdue University.</ref> '''sour guava''',<ref name=lim>Lim, T. K. ''Edible Medicinal and Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 3, Fruits.'' Springer. 2012. pg. 728-29.</ref> '''Guinea guava'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PSGU3|taxon=Psidium guineense|accessdate=15 October 2015}}</ref> ([[English language]]), '''''Goyavier du Brésil''''' ([[French language]]),<ref name=pier>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/psidium_guineense.htm ''Psidium guineense''.] USFS. Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER).</ref> '''''brasiliaanse koejawel''''' ([[Afrikaans]]), '''''Stachelbeerguave''''' ([[German language]]), '''''chobo''''', '''''diondan''''' ([[Bolivia]]), '''''guayabillo de tierra fria''''' ([[El Salvador]]),<ref name=lim/> '''''araçá do campo''''', '''''aracahy''''' ([[Brazil]]), '''''guayaba brava''''', '''''sacha guayaba''''' ([[Peru]]), '''''allpa guayaba''''' ([[Ecuador]]), '''''guayaba agria''''' ([[Colombia]], [[Venezuela]], [[Mexico]]), '''''guayaba acida''''', '''''chamach''''', '''''pichippul''''' ([[Guatemala]]), '''''guísaro''''' ([[Costa Rica]]), and '''''guayabita de sabana''''' ([[Panama]]).<ref name=purdue/>

==Distribution and habitat==
This plant is native to the Americas, where its natural range extends from Mexico to [[Argentina]], and includes parts of the [[Caribbean]]. It has been widely [[introduced species|introduced]] outside of this range, and it is cultivated in some places. It is [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in parts of [[India]].<ref name=purdue/>

The plant grows best on sunny sites with moist, fertile soils, but it is tolerant of a wide range of conditions and can grow in disturbed areas and in bad soils. It does not tolerate [[salinity]] or flooded substrates.<ref name=lim/> In Brazil it is most common in coastal areas.<ref name=fern>Fernandes, T. G., et al. (2012). [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3349319/ In vitro synergistic effect of ''Psidium guineense'' (Swartz) in combination with antimicrobial agents against methicillin-Resistant ''Staphylococcus aureus'' strains.] ''The Scientific World Journal'' 158237.</ref>

==Description==
This plant can be a [[shrub]] 1 to 3 meters tall or a tree reaching 7 meters. The bark and foliage are grayish. The leaves are up to 14 centimeters long by 8 wide. The stiff, oval-shaped blades sometimes have toothed edges. The undersides are very glandular and are coated in pale or reddish hairs. Flowers grow in the leaf axils, singly or in clusters of up to 3. The flower has a white corolla and many [[stamen]]s.<ref name=purdue/> It is fragrant.<ref name=pier/> The fruit is firm, rounded, and up to 2.5 centimeters wide. It has a yellow skin, a yellow outer pulp and whitish inner pulp containing many seeds.<ref name=purdue/>

==Fruit==
The pulp of the fruit is said to have a tart, [[strawberry]]-like taste.<ref name=purdue/> It has also been described as bitter.<ref name=pier/> Different varieties have different tastes, and some are sweet enough to eat as raw fruit.<ref name=lim/> They make good [[fruit preserves]].<ref name=purdue/>

This species has been crossed with its relative, the [[Psidium guajava|common guava]]. The resulting fruits are small, but numerous.<ref name=purdue/>

==Other uses==
The wood of the plant is hard and sturdy and can be used as [[lumber]] and to make durable objects like tool handles. The bark has [[tannin]] and can be used in [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]].<ref name=purdue/>

There are a few medicinal uses for the plant. Extracts of the bark and roots are used to treat [[diarrhea]] in Brazil. Extracts of the leaves are used to ease the [[common cold]] in [[Costa Rica]].<ref name=purdue/> Laboratory studies show that extracts have some activity against [[Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus|methicillin-resistant ''Staphylococcus aureus'']], particularly when combined with antibiotics. [[Flavonoid]]s identified in the plant include [[quercetin]], [[avicularin]], and [[guaijaverin]].<ref name=fern/>

==Ecology==
The plant is a host for the [[mistletoe]] ''[[Psittacanthus angustifolius]]''.<ref name=mel>Melgar, J. and M. Berrios. (2001). [http://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/2001/October/Pages/85_10_1120.1.aspx First report of ''Psittacanthus angustifolius'' on ''Psidium guineense'' and ''Pinus tecunumanii'' in Honduras.] ''Plant Disease'' 85(10) 1120.1.</ref>
